name: Colon cleansing

image.caption: Trip to India - Colon cleansing anyone?

lead: Colon cleansing covers a range of methods intended to clear the colon: oral regimens of fibre, herbs or laxatives, enemas, and colonic irrigation in which water is passed through the rectum. People looking to improve their appearance use it hoping for a flatter, less bloated midsection and clearer-looking skin.

Its supporters rest the idea on autointoxication, the belief that waste in the colon causes ill health. Mainstream medicine uses bowel preparation before colonoscopy and has studied those regimens extensively, while organisations such as the American Cancer Society state the evidence does not support cleansing as a treatment for disease.

paras: Practitioners use oral products such as fibre, herbs or laxatives, cleansing enemas held for a few minutes, or colonic irrigation sessions with specialised equipment. It is often combined with detox diets.

Reported harms include dehydration, electrolyte depletion, disrupted gut flora, rectal perforation and infection from poorly sterilised equipment; coffee enemas were linked to deaths in 1980 reports. Herbal products can interact with medicines, and a case report describes colitis induced by a cleansing agent.

chain: Laxative, enema or irrigation empties the bowel
Less stool and gas in the abdomen
angle.text: Users cleanse the colon hoping to look leaner around the waist and to improve skin. Bowel emptying can temporarily reduce abdominal distension, which is the appearance payoff people seek.

lead: Colon cleansing, also called colon hydrotherapy or colonic irrigation, is a group of practices aimed at emptying the colon through oral regimens, enemas or water irrigation.[1] In appearance-focused communities it is associated with reducing bloating, a flatter stomach and a clearer complexion, on the theory that clearing the bowel removes accumulated waste.

Proponents hold the idea of autointoxication, in which putrefied faeces in the colon cause nonspecific symptoms and poor health.[1] The term was coined in 1884 by French physician Charles Jacques Bouchard, and was promoted by some mainstream physicians in the late 1800s and early 1900s; a 1919 JAMA paper by W.C. Alvarez began the medical community's rejection of the hypothesis, and the practice resurged in alternative medicine from the 1990s.[1]

Medicine uses its own colon cleansing before colonoscopy and imaging, and trials compare preparation regimens, such as split-dose versus day-before dosing.[2][3] The American Cancer Society says available evidence does not support colon therapy for cancer or other diseases, and the Mayo Clinic notes the colon normally expels waste.[1]
infobox: FDA regulates equipment, not oral supplements

paras: Colonic irrigation introduces water, sometimes with herbs, through the rectum with special equipment and repeats until the colon is clear. Oral regimens use fibre, herbs, supplements or laxatives, and cleansing enemas hold liquid in the colon for 5 to 15 minutes.[1] Mainstream medicine uses enemas for severe constipation and imaging, which the article distinguishes from colon cleansing.[1]

Proponents believe waste lining the colon harbours parasites or harmful bacteria and causes headache, fatigue and irritability.[1] Critics reply that such symptoms can come from mechanical bowel distension as in irritable bowel syndrome.[1]

Ancient Egyptians and Greeks held beliefs the idea later built on. Ilya Mechnikov (1845-1916) supported it, and the medical rejection followed a 1919 paper.[1] Internet marketing and infomercials for oral products grew in the 2000s.[1]

Cleansing before colonoscopy is a distinct medical use. A meta-analysis found split-dose preparations superior to day-before regimens,[3] and a systematic review compared oral bowel preparations.[4] The Medical Letter reviewed colon cleansing products in 2009.[5]

Colonic irrigation can disrupt gut flora, and frequent use can cause dehydration and electrolyte depletion.[1] Rare serious harms include rectal perforation and amoebic infection; a 1982 amebiasis outbreak was linked to a chiropractic clinic, and coffee enemas were linked to deaths in 1980 reports.[1] A case report describes colitis induced by a cleansing agent.[6]
In the United States the FDA regulates colon-hydrotherapy equipment production but not its use or oral supplements, and has issued warning letters over claims, safety and quality control.[1]

Studies concern medical bowel preparation rather than wellness cleansing. Trials and meta-analyses compare regimens for colonoscopy,[3][4] and a randomized trial examined mechanical colon cleansing for screening colonoscopy.[7] No studies found testing colon cleansing for appearance outcomes.
